text: Maddalena Casulana (c. 1544 – c. 1590) was an Italian composer, lutenist, and singer of the late Renaissance, recognized as the first female composer to have had a complete book of her music printed and published in Western music history, dedicated to her female patron Isabella de' Medici.[1][2] Very little is known about her personal life beyond what is revealed in dedications and writings related to her madrigal collections. She was likely born in Casole d'Elsa, near Siena, based on her name, and received her musical training and early experiences in Florence.[3] Her first work appeared in 1566 with four madrigals in the collection Il Desiderio, also produced in Florence. Two years later, in 1568, she published her first full book of madrigals for four voices, Il primo libro di madrigali, marking the first printed and published work by a woman in Western music history. That same year, Orlando di Lasso conducted Nil mage iucundum at the court of Albert V, Duke of Bavaria in Munich; however, the music has not survived. Casulana maintained a close relationship with Isabella de' Medici, dedicating music to her in 1570, 1583, and 1586, all published in Venice. During this period, she married a man named Mezari, though no further details about him or their residence are known. Based on dedications, she visited Verona, Milan, and Florence, and likely went to Venice, as her music was published there and numerous Venetians commented on her abilities. She also made at least one trip to the French imperial court in the 1570s.[4] In the dedication to her first book of madrigals, she expressed her view on gender and artistic ability: "[I] want to show the world, as much as I can in this profession of music, the vain error of men that they alone possess the gifts of intellect and artistry, and that such gifts are never given to women." Her style is moderately contrapuntal and chromatic, similar to early works by Marenzio and madrigals by Philippe de Monte, but avoids the extreme experimentation of Ferrara school composers like Luzzaschi and Gesualdo. Her melodic lines are singable and carefully aligned with the text, and she favored dramatic dialogue in her polyphonic works, as seen in the madrigal "Morte - Che voi - Te Chiamo?", where she alternates voices to emphasize the text's questions and answers.[3] Composers such as Philippe de Monte held her in high regard, and the fact that Lassus conducted a work of hers at a wedding in Bavaria indicates his admiration. A total of 66 madrigals by Casulana have survived. In 2022, it was announced that 17 additional madrigals had been discovered, with twelve of them performed for the first time in 400 years on 8 March 2022 by the Fieri Consort as part of BBC Radio 3's International Women’s Day programming.[5][6][7] These discoveries were made by Laurie Stras, Professor of Music at the Universities of Southampton and Huddersfield, who identified the lost alto partbook of Casulana's 1583 five-voice madrigal book in the Russian State Library in Moscow, believed to have been looted from the Gdańsk Library of the Polish Academy of Sciences during the Second World War and still bearing Gdańsk's catalogue numbers.[6] The index includes a list of Casulana's works with references to original publications and available recordings in the third column.
